t: Aditiya Varma's family adopted into Venad
x: Aditiya Varma, his mother Makayiram Tirunal and his sister Asvati Tirunal are adopted into the ruling family of Venad. They came from the Vellarappalli kovilakam in Cochin; Makayiram was sister of Unni Kerala Varma, muppu of the Jayasimhanad (Quilon) house. She becomes first princess (Rani) of Attingal, Asvati second princess.
Aditiya Varma succeeds as king of Travancore (Venad).
Childless, the king's sister Asvati Tirunal, on whom the succession depends under marumakkathayam, adopts Ravi Varma, also from the Vellarappalli kovilakam of Cochin.

t: Aditiya Varma dies; the temple closes
x: Aditiya Varma dies at Neyyatinkara. Ravi Varma is a minor and the pillamar refuse to pay him their dues. Without money the king cannot pay the Nanjanad tribute, so the Madurai Nayk invades and the south-east empties of people. Unable to make the donations needed to become kulasekhara perumal, the crown lets the Padmanabhaswami Temple close. The temple council loses weight and the pillamar's military assembly, the desakuttam, becomes 'a sort of parliament' that chooses kings.
q: The desakuttam became in fact a sort of parliament which finally became so powerful that it chose from the various pretenders to the Travancore throne that candidate who offered them most privileges.

x: Asvati Tirunal declares herself regent, works to reopen the Padmanabhaswami Temple and forces the pillamar to pay homage and dues; several officials are punished.

t: Pillamar call in Kerala Varma of Nedumangadu
x: The pillamar turn to prince Kerala Varma of Nedumangadu, ruler of the rich hill principality the Dutch called the 'pepper-storeroom of Malabar'. He claims to be muppu of the Trippappur house and calls the 1672 adoption of Ravi Varma illegal. To strengthen his claim he is adopted by the Cheraway prince of Kayamkulam the same year.
q: The Dutch called it the "pepper-storeroom of Malabar".

x: At the end of 1677 the army of the pillamar and the Nedumangadu prince defeats Asvati Tirunal's forces. She flees with the boy king Ravi Varma to Varkalai, about 10 km north of Anjengo. Her mother, the Attingal rani, dies while negotiating, and the Nedumangadu prince seizes the regalia and proclaims himself king.

t: Asvati adopts the prince of Kottayam
x: A young Kolathiri prince of Kottayam, a poet and soldier passing Attingal on pilgrimage to Rameswaram, is adopted by Asvati as her son (a 1734 Dutch account says he had been her lover) and made prince of Iranyal, the second prince's title. He defeats the pillamar and the collateral princes; Asvati returns to Trivandrum with him as co-regent.
src: Notitie vant nieuws uijt de rijken van Trevancoor (c.1732), VOC 2234; Van Meeckeren, Korte beschrijving (1734)

t: Ravi Varma comes of age at Kalkulam
x: Ravi Varma reaches his majority and becomes king at Kalkulam. He reigns twenty years but weakly; the prince of Kottayam remains the real power.

To pay for an army that does not depend on the nobles, the prince of Kottayam promotes trade to raise chumkam (customs) and introduces a new kaliyan panam, probably minted at Iranyal, against the pillamar's private mints. The same year Asvati grants the English a factory at Idathara near Quilon; the pillamar side with the Dutch and the English leave in January 1686.

t: Failed Kolathiri adoption; pillamar bring in Madurai
x: Idathara Potti is sent to Cannanur to adopt Kolathiri princes, but the two princesses who arrive turn out to be of the wrong branch, probably sabotaged by the pillamar. The pillamar ally with the Madurai Nayk, who invades for tribute. When the Nayk proves dangerous to them too, they change sides; the united army beats the Nayk at Tiruvattar, north of Kalkulam.

t: Peace; the prince of Kottayam builds cavalry and artillery
x: At the March 1688 peace the pillamar try to make the Nedumangadu prince second prince; Asvati thwarts the ceremony. The prince of Kottayam raises cavalry with horses captured from Madurai and uses artillery captured from the Dutch, and later in the year subdues the pillamar and Nedumangadu.

t: First Dutch pepper contract with Travancore
x: The prince of Kottayam concludes the first pepper contract with the VOC, offering a fortified trading post in exchange for military support. The Dutch never give the support because he keeps raising customs to pay his army, which frustrates trade. In 1691 he also marries a Kolathiri princess to the prince of Pandalam.
The rebels' leader dies, but the pillamar keep fighting by attacking the Europeans the prince depends on.

t: Pillamar burn Dutch Anjengo and Tengapattanam
x: The pillamar force the Dutch to abandon Anjengo, which is plundered and burnt; at Tengapattanam the Dutch resident Johannes Heidenberg is killed. The Dutch damage claim becomes the 'Attingal Debt' of 80,000 kaliyan panam (about 480,000 rupees), still demanded from Martanda Varma decades later.

t: Asvati crowns the prince of Kottayam
x: Asvati crowns the prince of Kottayam king, though Ravi Varma already reigns.

When the Karunagappalli prince dies, Kayamkulam invades, claiming to be muppu of the Cheraway house. If it took Karunagappalli the Cheraway lands would outweigh the Trippappur. A coalition under the prince of Kottayam, with Nedumangadu and Purakkad auxiliaries, drives Kayamkulam out and restores the dead prince's brother.

In the month of Karkadagam 871 KE, returning from Asvati's palace to his own Valia Koikal Palace, the prince is met by pillamar including Idathara Potti and Ilampel Pandarathil. Asked to sign a document, he sits down and is speared in the back, then cut down with swords. De Lannoy rejects the later sexual explanation: the real motive was his reforms.
q: The real reasons were the administrative reforms intended to strengthen central power to an extent unpalatable to the pillamar.

t: Asvati crosses the Karamana and adopts from Kolathiri
x: Asvati takes over Travancore as well as Attingal, crossing the Karamana river that custom forbade an Attingal rani to cross. She sends Edavai Pillai Mether to Kolathiri and adopts two princes, Aditiya Varma and Rama Varma, and four princesses. The youngest princess will be Martanda Varma's mother. At the end of 1696 she cedes Anjengo to the English.

Asvati dies. The eldest Kolathiri princess becomes rani of Attingal; Ravi Varma resumes rule. The pillamar ally with the Nayk, who invades in February. Ravi Varma buys over the Madurai officers with Kalkulam fort and lands, crushes the pillamar, then turns on the Madurai garrison.
Queen-regent Mangammal of Madurai sends general Narasappaya on a huge punitive invasion; he returns loaded with plunder. More raids follow for two years and ruin the country.

t: Koduman and Vanji Mutton rule in fact
x: The Dutch report that neither king nor rani has authority: the pillamar Koduman and Vanji Mutton of Pallichel collect customs, control trade and attack merchants who will not pay. In 1703 the Dutch speak of 'mere anarchy'.
q: due to the bad government of this king no merchant wants to live in his country
src: Cochin Council to Batavia, 1 Nov 1703; VOC 1674

t: Ravi Varma dies; the Neptune plundered
x: Ravi Varma dies; Aditiya Varma of Kolathiri should succeed, but the pillamar ignore the adopted princes. In June the English ship Neptune is wrecked at Manacore and plundered by the pillamar, though wrecks were crown property.

t: Pillamar choose the Nedumangadu prince as king
x: The pillamar choose the brother of Kerala Varma of Nedumangadu as king. Aditiya Varma looks to Karunagappalli for allies.

The Karunagappalli prince, remembered as 'the greatest idiot on the Malabar coast, interested only in admiring his elephants', is overwhelmed by his madumbimar and flees to Kayamkulam, which gets itself adopted into Karunagappalli.

t: Two Trippappur boys arrive in Karunagappalli
x: Regretting the Kayamkulam adoption, the Karunagappalli prince cancels it and, on the advice of Cochin, Purakkad and Tekkumkur, adopts two nephews of Aditiya Varma, neither older than 14. They arrive in two Purakkad ships and succeed in September.

t: Mammali Kitavus arrives from the Laccadives
x: Two ousted Muslim rulers of the Laccadives, Mammali Kitavus and Kunju Koyamu (Many Kurukkal), kin of the Cannanur Ali Rajas, take refuge with Aditiya Varma, who makes Mammali a revenue farmer to pay troops. Under him a palace and fort are built at Cariapattanam, 11 km from Colachel. At the end of 1707 the Nedumangadu prince dies in battle against his nephew, the Kayamkulam prince.

t: Aditiya Varma courts the Dutch; Madurai marches on Kalkulam
x: Aditiya Varma summons the Dutch resident to Colachel and promises protection. Madurai troops and the pillamar march on Kalkulam; Mammali, unpaid, turns pirate and in April seizes Purakkad and Kayamkulam ships carrying Dutch passes. The pillamar then switch back to the king, who pays off the Nayk. In December Mammali is arrested at Cochin and escapes.
q: this princeling, who is the son of Ali Radja, is so ruthless in levying taxation, that we request Your Highness to dismiss him

x: The Nedumangadu prince invades again with a large Madurai force; the pillamar change sides; the Dutch refuse to help. Customs are farmed to the English. Aditiya Varma flees to the court of Vatayattu Pillai at Quilon and in April marches back, bribing the Nayk's officers.
src: Cochin Council to Batavia, 15 Mar and 1 May 1709; VOC 1773

t: Desakuttam threatens to invite the French
x: The pillamar in their assembly threaten to give the French a factory at Cariapattanam unless the Dutch send a resident to Tengapattanam. The Dutch refuse until the war ends.
src: Council of the Pillamar to Barend Ketel, 21 Oct 1710; VOC 1807

t: Peace: Nedumangadu king, Aditiya Varma heir
x: Faced with a Kayamkulam threat to Karunagappalli, the rivals make peace: the Nedumangadu prince is king and Aditiya Varma second prince.

After the Nedumangadu prince dies, the pillamar choose Aditiya Varma as king with Chittra I of Nedumangadu as second prince. Peace in Travancore starts a civil war in Nedumangadu, where Travancore backs Chittra I and Kayamkulam his nephew. In July a Dutch resident returns to Tengapattanam.
With the rebel madumbimar, Kayamkulam ousts the Karunagappalli ruler; a coalition of Aditiya Varma, Cochin, Purakkad and Tekkumkur drives it out before the month ends.

t: Pillamar seize the Dutch factory at Tengapattanam
x: Alarmed by the king's success, the pillamar capture the newly reopened factory and imprison the resident; Kayamkulam uses the chaos to force its adoption into Karunagappalli.
The king remits a forty-year-old tribute; the pillamar promise to send their Madurai cavalry home and agree that 'the king should rule as his forefathers had done'.

t: Mint moved to Iranyal; debased panam
x: Aditiya Varma moves the mint from Kalkulam to Iranyal and forces a debased new kaliyan panam on the Kottar merchants, threatening to cut off their right hands and ears. He hires Tamil cavalry with the profit. When he punishes nayar of Chengara Pandarathil for refusing the coins, the pillamar turn against him.
Mammali Kitavus and his brother return and collect customs ruthlessly from Tengapattanam, plundering passing ships, even a royal one.

t: Chittra I dies; the Varma brothers quarrel
x: The death of Chittra I leaves Nedumangadu vacant. Aditiya Varma sends the Attingal rani and her son Chittra II there; Rama Varma claims it himself, backed by the pillamar. Kayamkulam and Desinganadu also claim it; the Nedumangadu madumbimar keep Chittra II out.

t: Fighting at Quilon over two cotton merchants
x: Royal troops under the prince of Neyyatinkara clash with Vatayattu Pillai's men in the Quilon suburbs after the prince fines two of the Pillai's merchants for selling cotton outside government channels.
Fear of Kayamkulam, which is stirring the Karunagappalli madumbimar, reconciles Aditiya Varma and Rama Varma.
Early in 1715 Aditiya Varma has his sister and her two sons, the prince of Neyyatinkara and the boy Martanda Varma, adopted into Karunagappalli to block Cheraway (Kayamkulam) influence there.

The Varma brothers visit the Cochin king and the Dutch commander Barend Ketel to ask for military help against the nobles. Ketel tells them the dissensions are rooted in the kingdom 'like a cancer'; Rama Varma complains the nobles want kings who 'sit on the throne like mute statues'. Even an offer of 120,000 kaliyan panam a year for a Dutch garrison is refused. Meanwhile Kayamkulam invades Karunagappalli and keeps the two adopted princes out.
q: The nobles only desire that the kings sit on the throne like mute statues and do only what the nobles wish them to do.
src: Report of a conference between Barend Ketel and the king of Travancore, 17 Apr 1715; VOC 1866

t: Pillamar offer the crown to Desinganadu
x: The pillamar back Desinganadu, head of the Jayasimhanad (Quilon) house, for the throne. He wants Dutch guarantees first. Aditiya Varma courts Colombo against Cochin; two Ostend ships trade arms for pepper at Colachel, alarming Ceylon governor Isaac Rumph. In August both Colombo and Cochin refuse to take sides.

t: Aditiya Varma dies; Anjengo seizes temple land
x: Aditiya Varma dies early in February. The English interpreter Ignatio de Malheiros seizes Kottadalli, temple land of Chirayinkizh at the Attingal river mouth. Koduman Pillai dies in late February and his rival Vanji Mutton rises, charging the English 500 panam to trade.

Three Hindu pepper merchants staying at De Malheiros's house are smeared with Ash Wednesday ashes by a maid-servant, a grave caste pollution. One wounds her; chief William Gyfford, who cheated the merchants with false weights, has their swords broken over their heads and expels them. Koduman's successor burns an English ship; Bombay sends six East Indiamen.
src: John Wallis, A short treatise on Attinga (1729); OIOC G/40/22

x: Gyfford, Simon Cowse and about 140 men go to present gifts to the new rani of Attingal, the princess of Kallada (Desinganadu's sister) whom the English had asked the pillamar to install. After the ceremonial volley, nayar seize their ammunition and kill them. Gyfford's tongue is torn out and he is nailed to a log and floated down the Attingal river. De Lannoy concludes the pillamar under Koduman's heir and Vanji Mutton did it, not Desinganadu or the king.
q: the most preposterous and unprecedented action as was ever heard of

x: News reaches Anjengo three days later. Chief gunner Samuel Ince takes command and blows the powder magazine; women and children board the Prosperous, which sails for Galle. The pillamar besiege the fort without success and burn its surroundings.
The rival houses celebrate peace at Onam, the first since 1713. In eight days of mock fights between nayar of the three swarupam, watched by the princes from a hill, 20 men are killed.

t: Rama Varma names his nephews; civil war with Chittra II
x: Rama Varma makes the prince of Neyyatinkara and Martanda Varma second and third prince, passing over Chittra II of Nedumangadu as a leper. War follows; Madurai sends 500 horse and 5,000 foot. Chittra II is restored but dies in December 1721; in January 1722 Neyyatinkara becomes second prince and Martanda Varma third.

t: Desinganadu allies with Kayamkulam; the Tellicherri prince adopted
x: Desinganadu leaves Attingal and adopts two princes and a princess from Kayamkulam's Cheraway house, which now claims Travancore, Nedumangadu and Karunagappalli. Rama Varma answers by adopting the exiled Kolathiri prince of Tellicherri and his sister; the Tellicherri prince becomes second prince, Martanda Varma fourth.

t: Attingal rani's contract with the English
x: The Kallada princess, as rani of Attingal, promises the English punishment of the murderers and pepper. The English, busy with the Angria pirates, do nothing; Rama Varma and the pillamar oust her and restore the legitimate rani.
Rama Varma defeats the army of the Madurai Nayk and the pillamar. Meanwhile Kayamkulam bribes the Karunagappalli madumbimar to make its third prince ruler there.

After offering the English a factory at Colachel on 25 April, Rama Varma signs a treaty with the East India Company. With English money, on Martanda Varma's advice, he hires Maravar cavalry from the Coromandel coast: outsiders with no local power base who could be sent home.

t: Vanji Mutton marches on Iranyal with Madurai
x: Vanji Mutton leads a huge army with the Madurai forces to Iranyal to collect a tribute of two elephants and 400,000 kaliyan panam. The king pays a quarter, borrowing from the English and the Kottar merchants, who have taken refuge in the Suchindram temple.

t: Pillamar destroy the English factory at Colachel
x: To cut the king off from English money and force him to dismiss his Maravar cavalry, the pillamar destroy the Colachel factory.

Marching to force tribute from Kayamkulam, Rama Varma's army, with cavalry, defeats Desinganadu's army, which has none, at Navaikulam near Quilon. 2,000 Travancore soldiers occupy the second Desinganadu prince's palace before Kayamkulam's help stops them. Armistice in November.

t: Factories offered and destroyed; French arrive
x: With loans from Anjengo's new chief Alexander Orme and the Kottar merchants (whose Suchindram refuge had been plundered by Madurai soldiers) the king keeps his cavalry. In April the English reopen Colachel; the pillamar destroy it again. In July Rama Varma offers them a wing of his new palace-fort at Cariapattanam. In December a French ship comes to Colachel.

t: French offered Vizhinjam; pillamar and Madurai overrun the south
x: The French are offered Vizhinjam and Cariapattanam. Unable to repay the English or pay Madurai, the king loses large tracts at the end of February to the pillamar and the Nayk. In August Vanji Mutton writes that he is master of Attingal.
Out of money, Rama Varma discharges the Maravar. In March the pillamar defeat the royal troops and take Attingal, the mother-house of the dynasty. The king allies with Purakkad.

Royal forces under the prince of Neyyatinkara destroy Pallichel, south of Trivandrum, the seat of Vanji Mutton, who flees to Desinganadu. When the king negotiates with the Dutch, the English blockade the royal harbours and join the pillamar.

t: The Attingal rani flees; Capee palace burnt
x: After a renewed pillamar invasion the rani flees again to Rama Varma at Trivandrum. Her palace at Capee, between Edavai and Anjengo, is burnt by Mandacca Pillai, Vanji Mutton's heir.

t: The Kilimanur prince murdered on the Attingal road
x: Between March and November 1728, hurrying back to Attingal, the rani's retinue is stopped by the pillamar. They kill her husband Kerala Varma of Kilimanur before her and her small son, the future Rama Varma (r.1758-98); she is dragged from her palanquin by her hair. On 25 March Kayamkulam and Desinganadu had declared for the pillamar.
q: Deeper offence to the mother of the lineage was unthinkable.

t: Pepper offered to the Dutch and the French
x: Seeking revenge, Rama Varma offers the Dutch pepper at Tengapattanam (they want it at Quilon and refuse) and drafts free trade for the French at Colachel.

Rama Varma dies of smallpox; the prince of Tellicherri, his successor, dies on 28 February. The prince of Neyyatinkara becomes king. In March Martanda Varma flees to Attingal with the treasury, and the English arm the pillamar-Desinganadu coalition.
The English agree to supply the pillamar with brimstone and saltpetre in exchange for pepper.

After six months the prince of Neyyatinkara dies of smallpox at Tiruvattar. His younger brother Martanda Varma, then at Attingal, becomes king. Three successions in a year have left the kingdom in chaos.

t: Hunted king; the Tambi brothers revolt
x: Martanda Varma, 24, son of the youngest Kolathiri princess and a Kilimanur prince, is pursued so hard that legend has him sleeping in treetops. The pillamar leave Desinganadu for Pappu Tambi and Rama Tambi. De Lannoy argues from a 1742 letter of Martanda Varma that the Tambis were sons of his brother the prince of Neyyatinkara, not of Rama Varma as usually said. On 25 October the king makes terms with Desinganadu, who pays 6,500 kaliyan panam and returns an elephant.
q: the Desinganadu, the Tambi, son of our deceased brother, the Mutaliyar and the madumbimar united against me
src: Martanda Varma to Paliyath Achan, 23 Mar 1742; VOC 2564

t: Pillamar and Tambis beaten at Iranyal
x: The coalition attacks the mud-walled royal fortress of Iranyal between Colachel and Kalkulam, which with Kalkulam controls the rice and cloth of the south and the Kottar trade. They are defeated: 'a turning point in the royal struggle with the nobility'. Martanda Varma captures the Neyyatinkara prince's concubine and children, but Rama Tambi escapes.
Alexander Orme of Anjengo brings English presents and asks for a factory at Kottar or Colachel; the king says he will think about it.

The Tambis tell the Nayk Vijayaranga Chokkanatha that Martanda Varma is a usurper who closed Towalla (Tovala) to Madurai tribute collectors. Madurai sends 300 to 400 horse and 600 foot. The king holds Kalkulam; in April he destroys Kottar (and the Dutch resident's house) and Cariapattanam is destroyed. The rebels seize ships at Tengapattanam for ransom.

The prince of Desinganadu dies; Kayamkulam claims the Quilon throne for its nephew, adopted in 1722. English and Indian merchants smuggle cannon to Kayamkulam through Colachel, some hidden in hollow trees.
Having lost Kottar and its revenue, the king flees with the Attingal rani to the court of Vatayattu Pillai at Quilon de Sima.

t: Madurai troops run wild; the pillamar recall the king
x: In June the king's invitation to Kayamkulam and Vadakkumkur for an alliance is declined. Then the Madurai general dies, his unpaid troops plunder the country, and by late July the pillamar drive them back over a pass. They offer Martanda Varma the throne; he returns to Trivandrum in September.

After a fight at Neyyatinkara (60 killed and wounded), the new Madurai general Alagappa Mudaliyar asks the king to justify himself. Ramayyan, later dalawa, and Narayana Iyen explain matrilineal succession; the general rejects the Tambis' claim and imposes peace.
q: the nephews inherit the uncles' property, that the kings marry from families inferior to themselves in caste, that the sons begotten of such union have therefore no title of succession

x: At four in the afternoon the Tambi brothers visit the king at Kalkulam and are killed by his men. In the legend Pappu Tambi is stabbed in the back by a sentry, and Martanda Varma himself kills Rama Tambi and throws his body from the window.

The pillamar plan to murder the king at the Panguni Uttaram festival in Trivandrum and offer the crown to the new Desinganadu. An innkeeper reports their secret meeting seven miles south of Trivandrum; messengers are seized. At the festival the plotters are arrested, tried at Nagercoil palace, and executed or banished. Their lands are confiscated and sold; only Vatayattu Pillai is spared and made hereditary general of Attingal.
q: There has lately been discovered a conspiracy in Attinga of murdering the king of Travencore and bringing in the king of Quilones forces
src: Anjengo Factory Records, 15 Dec 1730; OIOC G/1/21

x: Polluted by killing kin and nobles, Martanda Varma uses confiscated wealth for penance: he completes the temple's rebuilding with the Brahmin architect Balakantara, builds 108 Brahmin houses, and revives the daily Puspanjali puja, adding an evening one at Suchindram for his victory. The Vettai (hunt) and Arat (sea bath) processions re-enact Vishnu destroying the demon, which De Lannoy reads as yearly symbolic killing of the Tambis and pillamar.

Vijayaranga Chokkanatha dies without a son; his widow Minakshi's adoption is challenged with the Nawab of Arcot's help. Weavers and artisans flee to Travancore, raising customs income, with which Martanda Varma enlists 1,000 Maravar mercenaries, mostly cavalry, under Ponnam Pandya Thevar. Madurai raids weaken.

The army crosses the Kallada river into Nedumangadu and takes a fort from the Desinganadu-Kayamkulam garrison. A Dutch envoy, the merchant Carma Kumatti, is told the 1691 contract is void because the prince of Kottayam was a usurper.

After 10,000 and then 15,000 to 20,000 Travancore troops gather at Quilon, the combined Kayamkulam-Desinganadu army is beaten near Quilon. Desinganadu's palanquin is briefly captured. On 26 March his men are driven from the small fort of Peramur, and Martanda Varma plunders the sanctuary pagoda holding his treasure, breaking the custom of temple refuge.

Restrained from burning his own palace at Kallada, Desinganadu flees at two in the morning to Kayamkulam with his family and Vanji Mutton. The queen-mother and second prince submit. On 31 March the Dutch envoys Teeling and Finia meet the king at Aivika on the Kayamkulam beach; he demands 65 years of tribute from Kayamkulam.

After the armies march on Panderatourte north of Quilon, Kayamkulam agrees with Dutch help to pay 51,200 Quilon panam once and 12,000 a year, give two elephants (one as a fine for firing at the king) and evacuate Kunattur, Carama and Chericol in Karunagappalli. On 22 April at Kallikkattu Tura, Travancore promises the Dutch to send Madurai weavers home and trades a captured tiger for two gold-ribboned hats; the Dutch get paid guards (changatam) at Tengapattanam.

t: Kayamkulam reneges; Travancore marches on Aivika
x: Probably encouraged by the Cochin king, Kayamkulam refuses to carry out the treaty. Travancore sends 11,000 foot and 1,000 horse to Aivika. The Dutch refuse Kayamkulam money and powder; pepper gardens have been destroyed and the merchants are lending to the king instead of advancing to weavers. A tax collector is posted at Anjengo's gate.
q: the pacification of the restless Malabar kings is seldom of long duration

x: At Vatayattu Pillai's court, before the Dutch and envoys of Nedumangadu, Cochin and Purakkad, Desinganadu signs peace with Travancore and pays tribute.

With the treasury empty and Madurai invading from the south, Martanda Varma withdraws from Karunagappalli. In March he offers Desinganadu peace if he demolishes his lines near Quilon and returns a princess Vanji Mutton had kidnapped from Attingal; refused.

Fearing Travancore, the Cochin king backs Kayamkulam. On 18 April the Dutch threaten to bombard Travancore's ports unless it supplies pepper. In May the Cochin king meets the Kayamkulam and Purakkad princes at Tiruvalla to plan an attack on Karunagappalli.

To pre-empt Kayamkulam, Cochin sends the Tekkumkur kaimal into Karunagappalli; Kayamkulam and Desinganadu then cross the border and defeat both the kaimal and Martanda Varma's sister the rani, who flees to him and dies at the end of May. Chericol and Carama are reoccupied. Short of money, the king stays out.

t: Free trade for the English; a refuge-fort at Mondy
x: From July the king offers the English free trade in piece-goods under a royal supervisor. The money pays for a fortress-palace at Mondy near Paravur as a refuge, and for European military specialists.

t: Vizhinjam chank fishery to the English
x: Madurai troops again hold Travancore back in February and March; the king probably pays them off with English money, granting the East India Company the chank (conch) fishery at Vizhinjam. The chank is the emblem of Travancore.
To avenge his sister and free Karunagappalli, 1,500 men march from Trivandrum to the Quilon suburbs as an advance guard, followed by a main army of 20,000.

The second prince of Desinganadu is defeated at Kallada; Desinganadu flees with his mother into Quilon. On 20 May, with Dutch mediation urged by Cochin, he makes peace: 9,000 Quilon panam, neutrality in the Kayamkulam war, Kallada returned. The Dutch get leave for a pepper store at Panderatourte inside the war zone.

The king arrives at Mavelikara, the Karunagappalli princes' court, to observe his dead sister's anniversary. Dutch envoy Ezechiel Rabby, a leading Jewish merchant of Cochin, hears Kayamkulam's peace ideas: lease back the Karunagappalli lands and adopt two Travancore princes.

At dawn Travancore horsemen enter the Kayamkulam lines. On the advice of his second madumbi Cattenatta the prince goes out sword in hand; Cattenatta and the bodyguard desert him and he is surrounded and killed. De Lannoy suspects treason benefiting Cochin and Desinganadu, who now becomes first prince of Kayamkulam, uniting Quilon and Kayamkulam.

Bound by custom to avenge his uncle, Desinganadu sends chaver, nayar sworn to die, to kill the king. Afraid of them, Martanda Varma pulls back from Karunagappalli to Trivandrum, and the Karunagappalli madumbimar go over to Desinganadu. In July Julius Valentijn Stein van Gollenesse had become commander of Cochin.
q: like madmen run upon the point of their enemies' swords, which make them be generally dreaded by all

x: War resumes when the monsoon ends. Desinganadu's ally Nedumangadu sends auxiliaries, defeated at Caddebenath.

t: Mooyaard's mission; 300 Dutch soldiers asked for
x: Dutch envoy Johannes Mooyaard meets the king at Carnapoli (Karunagappalli). The king answers Desinganadu's demand for blood-money by recalling that Kayamkulam had once killed the Nedumangadu prince. He offers 1,000 candies of pepper for 300 VOC soldiers, both to modernise his army and to deny Desinganadu Dutch help.

His treasury nearly empty, Desinganadu agrees peace: south Cheritali in Karunagappalli for him, Chericol for Travancore, and 25,000 kaliyan panam a year tribute. He then refuses the Dutch a grain of pepper.

Nedumangadu asks the Dutch for help; they forward his letter to Martanda Varma, who uses it as a reason to invade. Prince Kerala Varma and his whole family are imprisoned, a break with the custom that a defeated prince only paid tribute. In October the king farms Nedumangadu's pepper for 80,000 kaliyan panam to Madewi Chetti, who ships it over the hills to Coromandel. The English are offered Vizhinjam.

After the Afghan victory over the Safavids (1722), Muscat, Sind and Gujarat traders shift to Malabar, and private European traders keep prices high. The Dutch get almost no pepper. Stein van Gollenesse decides Desinganadu, ruling Quilon and Kayamkulam, should be the barrier against Travancore.
With open VOC support Desinganadu allies with the Cochin king and Tekkumkur. Martanda Varma builds the Aramboli Lines against Madurai raiders on the south-east border, paid for by pepper and cloth.

The governor of Ceylon, Gustaaf Willem van Imhoff, arrives with over 300 men to overawe the Malabar princes. On 18 February at Mattancherri the Cochin king, still claiming Karunagappalli, urges action against Travancore.
q: After two notable revolutions, the first inside, the second outside his kingdom, and also by two profitable wars this king has grown to ascendancy

t: Martanda Varma meets Van Imhoff on the beach at Tengapattanam
x: Called for eight, the king arrives at half past eleven at night on horseback, dressed as a bhattan from his Arat rites. In four hours on a podium facing away from the sea he accuses the Dutch of waiting to strike him, refuses a fixed pepper contract, and offers pepper only for help against Chanda Sahib over Shencotta. De Lannoy notes that other accounts of this meeting rest on Anquetil du Perron's 1771 Zend-Avesta, full of errors, not the Dutch diary.
q: His Highness is rather tall and has a keen mind so that he is able to impress the persons he meets
src: Diary of Van Imhoff, 25 Feb 1739; VOC 2472

x: The envoys will not sign the Dutch draft; they take it to the king on pilgrimage at Rameswaram, and ask for 10,000 kalanju of gold for his hiranyagarbha rite. Van Imhoff, amused and contemptuous, sends eight. The ceremony is only performed in January 1753.

Colachel merchants will not sell pepper without royal leave. The envoys return: the king will not sign and will not meet Stein van Gollenesse at Quilon on 14 March; the English pay 57 rupees a candy and supply arms. Desinganadu asks the Dutch for troops.

From Colombo Van Imhoff writes to Batavia that the balance should be restored by conquering Nedumangadu and Karunagappalli and supporting Cochin, Desinganadu and Vadakkumkur. On 10 September the king complains to him of the 'bad whisperings' at Cochin; Van Imhoff replies that the Company will tolerate no more insults.

Martanda Varma captures four wild elephants in a Nedumangadu pass. Elephant capture (anapiti) is a royal privilege, so Desinganadu, also claiming Nedumangadu, sends 300 men to block the pass; Travancore sends 3,000. On 4 September the king tells Cochin he has taken two villages of Desinganadu that belong to the Padmanabhaswami temple.

The VOC allies with Desinganadu, Cochin, Purakkad and Tekkumkur, probably at Cochin. Travancore already holds most of Desinganadu's lands including his lines south of Quilon. On 6 October 300 soldiers go from Cochin to Quilon fort; the king blocks the passes, places artillery, asks the English for arms and the French at Mahé for help.
q: That king uses all means to deceive the Company, pretending that he wanted only the best for us. But all these dissimulations will not blind us

x: Two European and two Indian companies under captain Joannes Hackert arrive from Ceylon, ordered to support Desinganadu 'without the slightest delay'. They attack the Travancore troops in the Quilon lines, demanding the return of 12 guns taken from Desinganadu's palace. The English send a little powder to Travancore.
src: Diary Hackert, 18 Oct 1739 to 8 Jun 1740 (Madras Dutch Records no. 10)

t: Magazine explodes in the Quilon lines
x: For weeks the Travancoreans rebuild by night what the Dutch destroy by day. Then a grenade hits their powder magazine and they flee in panic; the Dutch take 16 guns. On 24 November the Dutch camp at Paravur.
A Dutch spy reports about 5,000 foot and 70 horse entrenched on the Varkalai heights with six guns and some 50 English soldiers, probably gunnery instructors.

With Paliyath Achan's Cochin troops the Dutch cross into Nedumangadu and march on its capital Kottarakkara. On 17 December the Nedumangadu madumbimar submit to the coalition. Desinganadu, having got what he wanted, asks the Dutch to leave because they are 'spoiling the palm trees'; they withdraw to Paravur.

Travancore has pulled troops south to face Chanda Sahib, who comes early for tribute because his rival Vangara Tirumalai has allied with the Marathas. Desinganadu occupies Varkalai and on 27 December performs ceremonies at the Navaikulam temple, perhaps to be installed as its and Nedumangadu's protector.

t: March on Varkalai; fort Hollandia at Ayrur
x: The joint army marches along the beach past the English post at Edavai and up the steep Varkalai hill, dismounting its guns several times, burning houses and pagodas under Travancore protection. On 16 January at Ayrur the engineer Leslorant builds a small fort called Hollandia. Travancore holds Attingal under Krishna Anavy and Martanda Pillai and asks the French, through Kolathiri and Pandalam, for help.

The Dutch march over Varkalai hill, reach Manambur at noon and rout a Travancore force into the jungle, then burn the surroundings. In February a false alarm at Navaikulam convinces them Desinganadu is using them to frighten tribute out of the people.

t: Edavai plundered; battle at the Karamana
x: The allies plunder the English post at Edavai, claiming it is Travancore's. Two days later they cross the Karamana river into Attingal and beat the Travancoreans; the Maravar cavalry commander is killed. Pursuing, the Dutch are ambushed by 800 men and lose two guns and 72 dead; Travancore loses 700.

t: Attack on the Attingal palace fails
x: The English, fearing for Anjengo, give the rani 17 small guns and send 150 soldiers, 500 flintlocks and six barrels of powder, tested before the heir Rama Varma, and lend money for the Madurai tribute. The coalition assault on Attingal palace collapses: of 8,000 Desinganadu soldiers only 800 return. Desinganadu nearly kills himself with his own sword. The allies fall back to Ayrur.

t: Arcot's army in the south; Suchindram plundered
x: Travancore fights the Nawab of Arcot's troops at Kanniyakumari; the heir Rama Varma leads reinforcements south. The Nawab rejects an offer of 120,000 kaliyan panam and six elephants. The temple tenants armed by the pottimar are beaten at Ittankad, 3 km from Suchindram, and the temple is plundered. Exiled pillamar plot with Madurai troops, proof they were not all killed.

Three French ships arrive; the Jesuit Pedro Correa briefs them. French soldiers land to a joyful welcome and the king offers them a house, but Dirois at Mahé, at peace with the Dutch, orders them home.

3,000 to 4,000 Desinganadu soldiers with 150 Dutch under captain Berger march from Quilon to Kottarakkara. With Travancore's army in the south, the Nedumangadu madumbimar change sides and in May at Kallada submit to the princess-regent, who had been in exile in Tekkumkur. Leslorant fortifies Paravur as Seeburg.

t: The Nedumangadu prince dies in Kalkulam custody
x: Her elder brother, the first prince of Nedumangadu, dies a prisoner at Kalkulam; murder by Travancore is widely believed. Martanda Varma hurries to Kottarakkara for the cremation, which by custom strengthens his claim as heir.

The allies invade Karunagappalli, where Martanda Varma grew up and his younger sister rules; she flees to Nedumpuram in Tekkumkur. The Dutch let the Cochin king nominate two princes for adoption there. Cochin gets Karunagappalli, Desinganadu Nedumangadu.

Martanda Varma signs a contract ceding Colachel to the French king, with full jurisdiction and the right to buy pepper and cloth, hoping for arms and mediation with Chanda Sahib. The French order their captain not to supply arms against the Dutch.

Van Imhoff's plan: hold the coast, blockade every port to cut off customs and arms, and raid inland after the monsoon. De Lannoy calls it the limited view of a sea-borne empire, since pepper and cloth could go overland to Coromandel. The fleet bombards Colachel for two or three days; the people flee; 2,000 Travancore men are sent. The coast from Quilon to Kanniyakumari is blockaded.
q: These unanswerable proceedings against our nation are extreme shocking for us

x: The fleet leaves Cochin. On 14 February, aboard the Berkenrode, Desinganadu says he now wants to conquer Attingal. Wind prevents a landing at Colachel at first.
src: Diary of Stein van Gollenesse, 7 Feb to 18 Apr 1741; VOC 2543

x: At five in the morning, covered by ships firing close inshore, over 400 men (three grenadier and two Indian companies) land in two hours, losing 22 dead and 17 wounded. The Travancoreans fall back to the dunes, a palm forest, then behind the Catholic church. Sailors fire into the church and wound a Jesuit; five Jesuits are held aboard the Opperdoes. The plan: a European-style fort with 300 men commanding the road to Kottar.
q: That king is so haughty that we do not dare to bring him such message or letter because he can not be trusted

x: The council of war adopts Leslorant's plan for a fort with a brick bastion on the west, later three mud bastions and one of brick for 30 guns, the church as granary. A fortnight later the Dutch find Iranyal evacuated; the king has withdrawn into the hills.

In Nedumangadu Desinganadu had burnt the estates of the pro-Travancore Pallikal Kurup; his faction called in Martanda Varma, who took Kilimanur. After a three-hour battle the allies retake it and burn over 400 houses, but Desinganadu halts for the Bharani festival of Bhadrakali.

Spies report French flags and a strong garrison; the king has had hats put on sticks and muskets poked through loopholes. After a bombardment the Dutch land, burn houses and temples and take prisoners, selling those over 14 to the Company as slaves at 12.5 rixdollars, 20 for a nayar.
300 Travancore soldiers dressed like Europeans and armed with flintlocks, under the heir Rama Varma, appear before Colachel with 300 Maravar cavalry.

Over a thousand more Travancore troops arrive and reinforcements stream from Kalkulam to Iranyal, though nayar and Maravar are said to be quarrelling. Anjengo's interpreter Salvador Rodriguez warns that Inname Kumar Thevar, son of the Maravar chief, has been sent to lead a suicide assault, promised a palanquin if he lives. On 5 April the Dutch pull their field guns inside and start a water tank, since the fort has no water.

In the north the armies of Desinganadu and the Nedumangadu princess-regent defeat the Travancoreans at Tottacotta near Ayrur. Encouraged, Stein van Gollenesse decides to leave Colachel, appointing Hackert commander-in-chief, Leslorant superintendent of works, and Johan Christiaan Rijtel commander of 250 Europeans and 50 lascorins.

He sails for Quilon intending to take 200 of the garrison; Hackert protests and he takes 100. Next day a spy says the king knows and will attack. On 14 April a Desinganadu kariyakar deserts to Travancore with 150 flintlock men and 500 archers; others follow.

Desinganadu says it is against custom to invade a neighbour's country; really he is angry the Dutch will not back his claim to Nedumangadu. For money, arms and the country around Paravur he agrees to fight on. On 16 April Stein van Gollenesse meets the Nedumangadu princess-regent in exile at Manaddi, a refuge in Tekkumkur on the Kayamkulam border protected by Edappalli. On 17 April he sees the Purakkad prince at Karur near Ambalapuzha and boasts that 5,000 men could not take Colachel.

When nine guns are mounted on the new north and south bastions, three of them mud, they collapse. There is no lime to finish the water tank, food is short and soldiers foraging for it are killed. Hackert hires 400 mukkuva coolies after quarrels over who must build. Early monsoon storms on 20 and 21 April nearly wreck the ships; the Soetelingskerk loses almost all its anchors.

Carl August Duijvenschot, a German sergeant-trumpeter who came out on the Delfland in 1734 and to Malabar in 1739, deserts to Travancore. He will command all European mercenaries in Travancore service and direct the siege of Colachel.
note: Chapter V (p.157) dates this desertion 25 February 1741.

x: Contrary winds block the ordered move north to Quilon, so Hackert sails the other way, to Tuticorin, taking all the ships, nearly all the rice, powder and ammunition and most of the troops. Rijtel stays with 250 Europeans, 50 lascorins and two ensigns. Stein van Gollenesse calls Leslorant 'so incapable and malignant' that he 'demolishes today what he built yesterday'. Hackert even asks Ceylon to withdraw from Malabar altogether.
Shortly before the monsoon Martanda Varma visits the Adi Kesava temple at Tiruvattar to pray for victory. Two heavy guns, carriages and ladders are brought from Trivandrum.

Heavy artillery served by Dutch deserters and English soldiers opens on Colachel. Under Duijvenschot the siege is run 'in a European way' with batteries, gabions, trenches and casemates, the deserters empowered to punish runaways. The English supply powder, lend guns and four gunners, and send three shiploads of ammunition; the king promises them two forts between Anjengo and Tengapattanam.

t: Batteries on the beach cut off the sea
x: By mid-June the trenches are a pistol shot away. Rijtel reports batteries on the beach that make supply from the sea impossible; fetching water from the well risks one's life. About 20,000 men strangle the fort. On 19 June the Tuticorin council decides to relieve it via Kanniyakumari rather than attack Iranyal and Kalkulam.
q: It was amazing how fast the enemy had built these batteries on the beach. One morning they were suddenly there.
src: Relaas of sergeant Jan Christoffel Hartman, 16 Dec 1741; VOC 2523

x: Through monsoon mud, with coolies dying of smallpox, Hackert arrives. By mid-July he has 549 soldiers, 111 unfit, against 12,000 to 15,000 Travancoreans. Unpaid since 1739, officers ask leave to go home. Asked for paper for cartridges, Cochin sends the old payrolls of 1663 to 1680 that the cockroaches had been eating.
The Travancoreans blow two mines and assault; they are repulsed. The interpreter Dufuijt and a corporal sent by boat for help are betrayed by the mukkuva boatman and captured.

t: Hackert balks at the Aramboli Lines
x: 420 men march from Kanniyakumari to the Aramboli Lines, a huge palisade with guns running from the hills. Drums and horns sound, a Dutch gun fires by mistake, and Hackert orders a retreat over the protests of François d'Haenens and Hendrik Wendelin Koller. 'A soldier can lose his reputation either by imprudent actions or by cowardice.'

Travancore's dead fill the fort's trenches; now they use mines and paper rockets with burning fuses too. Rijtel says he will surrender within eight days without relief. Discouraged and hit by smallpox, many besiegers desert; at the end of July the king pulls most of his army back to Hernitte, south of Colachel. A fishermen's headman refuses to run supplies in by dhoni 'even for 10,000 rixdollars'.
Commander Rijtel is mortally wounded in the head and hands the keys to ensign Adolf Swarts. The same day, at Kanniyakumari, Eustache de Lannoy deserts from the Dutch army into Travancore service.

t: The drunken garrison and the first surrender
x: After burying Rijtel the soldiers get arrack, climb the walls singing and waving their hats. The thin Travancore screen thinks relief has come. Martanda Varma comes himself, asks them down, and 31 men lower themselves on ropes; finding no officers among them, he agrees a capitulation giving them free passage, armed, to Kanniyakumari.

t: Watch-towers, a filled moat, a failed mine
x: The besiegers fill the west moat with coconut shells, gourds and soil and build towers taller than the walls. Duijvenschot, with 22 deserters now in Travancore service, digs a mine under the east side; on 9 August it blows up their own entrenchments instead.
q: These scoundrels have learned this task so badly that the mine had a contrary effect

t: Dutch storm the lines at Cobolon
x: In the night about 400 men march out of Kanniyakumari to the lines near the hills, scale them with ladders after sunrise, force the gate and burn houses. Hackert finds the lines cleverly built, so that shells roll into a water ditch, perhaps by an English engineer. On 8 August, 60 km from Colachel, they retreat; the heir Rama Varma reoccupies the lines and seals the gate with mud.

t: The magazine in the church explodes
x: Between four and five in the afternoon a cannon ball hits the powder magazine in the church: 600 pounds of powder, most guns and grenades go up, the wooden barracks burn and all food is lost. The quartermaster of the Porca sees the flag dipped three times and three blasts. Fourteen guns open fire and Maravar cavalry under Ramayyan Dalawa attack. Bodies foul the well.

De Lannoy, a week in Travancore service, negotiates the surrender. Bookkeeper Karel Hendrix and ensign Bertram sign in the Travancore camp and hand the keys to the king. Promised free passage to Kanniyakumari, the garrison is instead taken to Iranyal and Kalkulam. De Lannoy states that the date of 9 August given by Kerala historians is wrong.
q: The date of 9 August which is generally referred to as the day of surrender by all Kerala historians is therefore not true.

t: Martanda Varma visits Colachel on his birthday
x: He leaves quickly, because of the stench and because a king of Brahmin status should not enter a place of Christians and their dead. 60 or 70 Maravar and 25 others guard it until it is demolished. On 16 August his envoy, the bhattan Wadivesaram Savindera Anavy, brings Kanniyakumari an ola dated 9 August condemning the Cobolon attack: the VOC is only a trading company with no business making war.

Cochin learns of Colachel's fall. Madurai has been under the Marathas since March, after they beat Chanda Sahib. Their governor Apaya Nayak will help Travancore only for all its treasure, and is angry because Travancore troops helped his rebel nephew Maylappa Mudaliyar take Valliyur and Panakuddi. In early September Madurai troops cross the border at Kanniyakumari and offer the Dutch an alliance; Hackert calls the governor the cruellest, most arrogant ruler there is.

Unpaid, hungry and deserting, soldiers plan a rebellion. When Hackert arrests three agitators, the men march on the prison and demand to be locked up too, until he talks them round. Ceylon orders evacuation.

Four ships carry troops not to Tuticorin but to Quilon; another 388 leave on 4 and 5 October and Kanniyakumari is demolished. A Cochin council of war blames Hackert, who is sent to Batavia and dies in captivity. Hartman says the king never expected to take Colachel and was astonished the Kanniyakumari force never came.

t: Cochin leaves the coalition; Karunagappalli retaken
x: The English spread a rumour that the Chinese have captured Batavia. The old Cochin king pulls out, telling Travancore the Dutch slaughtered cows in temples. The Karunagappalli madumbimar change sides; Martanda Varma retakes the principality, strips them of office, kills those who protest, and installs the official Kochu Mussad.

Maratha envoys offer the Dutch an alliance because Travancore refuses to pay the 1,000 Madurai horse and several thousand foot that helped at Colachel, costing 60,000 rupees a month; Martanda Varma replaces them with men from Nedumangadu, Karunagappalli and Kayamkulam. The Dutch decline the 'untrustworthy robbers'.

t: Colachel offered to the French again
x: A French ship at Colachel is offered the port as a factory, even with Dutch captives as soldiers, at the urging of the king's pro-French kin of Pandalam and Kolathiri. In December Vanji Mutton tells the Dutch of a plot: Trivandrum, Kilimanur and Attingal are weary of war taxes.

t: Guns from Anjengo, flintlocks from La Bourdonnais
x: The king gets heavy artillery from the English at Anjengo. At the end of January the French admiral La Bourdonnais sells him 500 flintlocks, 36 barrels of powder, 5,000 flints, 1,000 bullets and 100 shells, partly for pepper. A defensive treaty with Madurai brings 300 horse under Manjano Sahib, sworn to avenge a son killed by the Dutch.

Three Dutch companies under Stein van Gollenesse and 3,000 Desinganadu men march from Quilon and capture Kilimanur. On 1 February a six-week ceasefire is agreed. On 15 February the Dutch send terms: prisoners back, 1,000 candies a year, factories at Colachel and Tengapattanam, the Attingal Debt, jurisdiction over all Christians.

t: Poku Mussa meets Rabby at Anjengo
x: The king's favourite answers: prisoners back except deserters who chose his service (they would be hanged); 1,000 candies, 800 paid in coin and 200 in arms; no factory at his expense without proof; Christians are his and the temples' subjects; Karunagappalli and Nedumangadu are his. Traders have no right to meddle in Kerala politics. Rabby calls the proposals 'brutal and arrogant'.

t: Vecchur falls; captain Berger in command
x: Stein van Gollenesse, unwell, returns to Cochin. 12,000 Travancoreans take Vecchur near Varkalai, threatening Ayrur, Tottacotta, Kilimanur and Paravur. Martanda Varma offers Madurai 100,000 kaliyan panam and an elephant for 1,500 men to hold Nedumangadu; Apaya Nayak refuses.

With enough Maravar cavalry hired, the king opens a northern front in Desinganadu's home principality. No Dutch reinforcements come: the Chinese rising on Java absorbs them. The second prince of Desinganadu, a leper, sends spies to the Travancore camp every night.
q: He is not only disfigured bodily by leprosy but also mentally for every night he sends confidants in the Travancore camp

x: Duijvenschot and ten deserters besiege Kilimanur with four batteries. After the first Dutch brigades are pushed back, the nayar desert en masse; 'not 10 of them stayed together'. Desinganadu escapes by night to Tottacotta; by mid-April the Dutch fall back to Ayrur. Ten Nedumangadu madumbimar submit, and shortly before 13 April Travancore takes Kottarakkara.

Under Duijvenschot the Travancoreans besiege Ayrur and Paravur; both capitulate in early May without resistance. At Hollandia three Dutchmen in Travancore service appear on the ramparts; the commander yields for free passage and is made prisoner outside, as at Colachel. All Dutch forts in Nedumangadu are lost. Purakkad turns on the Dutch.

Desinganadu flees to the Tiruvalla pagoda and then Cochin, trying to keep his hereditary lands. Martanda Varma has Duijvenschot devastate Kayamkulam: churches, pagodas and palaces burnt, trees cut down. Its treasures are given to the temples, then taken back and coined to pay the army.

Duijvenschot leads 1,000 royal guards dressed, armed and drilled like Europeans, the kunju kudis. Purakkad sends 50 large boats, soldiers and brass cannon; the Cochin king hands government to his pro-Travancore nephew. Desinganadu's general Achyuta Warriar holds the city with 3,000 men; over 6,000 besiegers die. In late July, on English advice, with Duijvenschot ill and money short, the king withdraws. 'That was the end of fighting.'

Desinganadu makes peace at Manaddi, where the Nedumangadu princess-regent had lived in exile. He may return and keeps his Kayamkulam lands for eight years' tribute (60,000 Quilon panam) and an elephant, pledging Manaddi and Toddipela, and so recognises Travancore's suzerainty. De Lannoy says recent literature 'mistakenly' calls it the treaty of Mannar.
q: In recent literature this treaty is mistakenly called the treaty of Mannar.

t: Talks on a ship in the Attingal river
x: Martanda Varma negotiates in person near Anjengo, mocking the Cochin king, who 'did nothing else but drink and eat', and promising to punish Cochin and Tekkumkur for dragging the Dutch into the war.

Under the new commander Reinicus Siersma, Rabby and Silvester Mendes conclude peace at Mavelikara: all prisoners back, deserters later if unpunished; 1,200 candies of pepper a year at 54 rupees delivered at Panderatourte; arms at cost; factories at Colachel, Kottar and Tengapattanam; Catholic clergy banned; Dutch help against the French and Arcot, neutrality between Travancore and Desinganadu. On 25 May Siersma meets the king at Ambalapuzha, who wants timber for the ruined Quilon palace. Batavia refuses to ratify.

t: The Nawab of Trichinopoly threatens the south
x: Nizam Mulk Ali, Nawab of Trichinopoly, having beaten the Marathas in Madurai, reaches south Travancore in August to punish the plunder of temples and offers the Dutch an alliance; they decline. Martanda Varma soothes Cochin with presents. Desinganadu sees his chance.

Desinganadu allies with the Tekkumkur prince (capital Kottayam, rich in pepper and timber, run by 18 madumbimar and two kaimal) and four powerful kartakels holding fiefs in its far south. In breach of Mavelikara the Dutch send him lead and powder at his expense.

After asking the English whether the Dutch would intervene, and arguing that only new lands let him meet his Mavelikara pepper quota, the king sends 10,000 foot and 300 horse into south Tekkumkur, rising to 25,000 with Purakkad's rice and men. The kartakels fall back after a six-hour fight; houses and a palace of the Tekkumkur prince are destroyed. In April they submit.

Vadakkumkur's mad first prince is a toy of the second prince (Travancore's protege) and the third (the Dutch one, who gave them land at Vecchur for a factory). 6,000 Travancore soldiers come by boat over the Cochin river and the third prince submits; the king buys land and fortifies it. Troops withdraw in July.
Tekkumkur's indemnity lets Martanda Varma pay the Nawab, who withdraws. In September a peace at Mavelikara binds Tekkumkur to pay 10,000 kaliyan panam and an elephant and cede land near Vadakkumkur.

t: Kayamkulam invaded; Desinganadu flees Quilon in disguise
x: From Purakkad the army attacks Kayamkulam, then marches on Quilon. Desinganadu leaves Achyuta Warriar in command and slips out at night in disguise to Tekkumkur, then Cochin, where he begs the Dutch 'with tears in his eyes' for money and arms. The Dutch block the Cochin river against a Travancore advance. The king, ill, withdraws to Attingal.

t: Desinganadu back in Quilon; Quilon de Sima burnt
x: Back in Quilon and entrenched on an island near the Dutch fort, Desinganadu sallies out and burns Quilon de Sima, seat of Vatayattu Pillai, during a temple festival. Ramayyan Dalawa and 1,000 men destroy several Kayamkulam temples.

Travancore soldiers try to reap the paddy of the Tiruvalla temple, under Cochin's protection, a customary challenge. The priests drive them off with long sticks: no one may touch a Brahmin, and a stick blow is the worst affront to a nayar. Cochin sends 300 men. Angered by temple destruction, the people of Kayamkulam drive Ramayyan back to Paravur.

Despite illness the king summons the Nedumangadu madumbimar at Trivandrum for more men. A large army marches via Attingal and occupies much of Quilon and Kayamkulam, making the people pay for the troops. In February 1747 he rejoins the army in Kayamkulam. The Dutch secretly send Desinganadu money, rice, an artillery lieutenant and six gunners.

Nobles and rice merchants, hurt by restrictions imposed for fear of Travancore, have the Purakkad prince dismiss his pro-Travancore adviser Koccu Menon. Vadakkumkur's pepper, about a million pounds a year, goes east through Todupuzha and Karikod to Madurai.

t: De Lannoy at the siege of Quilon
x: Martanda Varma arrives at Quilon de Sima with Eustache de Lannoy and artillery specialists. After three weeks of mortar and cannon fire Desinganadu flees a second time, to Cochin, where he pawns a diamond-set golden snake belt to the Dutch for a pension. Unlike Duijvenschot in 1742, De Lannoy keeps the siege going for six months.

De Lannoy's men capture the Quilon lines; Achyuta Warriar dies in battle and the second prince of Desinganadu flees into the Dutch fort. 'So, the last remnant of ancien régime Travancore disappeared.' The Cochin king, urged to act, can only stammer 'The Hon. Company has to help me'; Purakkad hurries back to Travancore's side.
q: So, the last remnant of ancien régime Travancore disappeared.

x: A Tekkumkur succession quarrel brings the rebel second prince to Martanda Varma's court. Krishna Anavy and Ramayyan invade; a temple under the Zamorin's protection is destroyed and Calicut promises Tekkumkur money and men. At Purakkad Koccu Menon, restored under pressure, dies in prison at year's end, the Dutch think by poison. In November Travancore demands Desinganadu's extradition from Cochin.

Cochin's envoys broker terms in Tekkumkur: the rebel second prince returns with 80,000 kaliyan panam and a monthly allowance, and Tekkumkur cedes Kudumalur to Purakkad, so that the northern princes are set against each other.

The returning prince, with ten Travancore guards, is seized by his brother, his hands tied, and killed. Purakkad, fearing for Kudumalur, joins Travancore with fifty boats and crosses the Cochin river from the west while the army comes from the south. By 30 August Tekkumkur must pay 200,000 kaliyan panam, hand over its armed boats guarding the river, return temple treasure and give up its protectorate over temples. When it balks, Travancore fells and sells its forests and the prince flees to Cochin.

t: The Jews of Mattancherri flee into Cochin fort
x: With tension on Cochin's southern border, the Jewish merchants of Mattancherri move inside the fort and leave their valuables with VOC servants. Martanda Varma mocks their panic. In Vadakkumkur a ceasefire of 8 September lets the third prince pay tribute; Travancore sends him 50 bodyguards.

The Cochin king dies. His successor Rama Varma calls himself Perumpadappu muppu though he is senior only of his own branch; the Chazhur Tamban, senior of all five branches, claims the title and the Alangadu revenues. The Tamban marries into the regent of Vadakkumkur's family, making him indirectly Travancore's ally.

In April the king promises to help the Tamban, then falls ill again. The Anjengo interpreter reports he walks supported by two servants, his legs and thighs wasting, 'convinced that he is punished'. The book dates the illness 'from at least 1747 onwards'.
q: Above his waist the king is still fit, but his legs and thighs are affected and melt away. Now this king is convinced that he is punished.
note: Chapter V (pp.179, 183) dates the illness from the end of 1745.

t: Tiruvalla temple taken; the Tekkumkur lines
x: Recovered, the king punishes Purakkad, Tekkumkur and Vadakkumkur. He takes the Tiruvalla temple under Cochin's protection and performs ceremonies there as protector of temples. Tekkumkur's people are fined and put to forced labour on a defence line over 11 km long between Parunda and Comerottu near the Cochin river, joining 20 stockades; Rabby reports some 15,000 at work. Vadakkumkur's minister and 18 madumbimar go over; by November 1750 Purakkad, Tekkumkur and Vadakkumkur are all subject.

At Toravur north of Vaikom, the Cochin second prince, the Dutch fiscal Bowijn and major Van Wrisberg meet Poku Mussa and Ramayyan. The Tamban's claims go to the Brahmin court of Vaikom, eight mimamsakas under the priestly prince of Edappalli.

With 1,500 Travancore auxiliaries the Tamban crosses the Cochin river and occupies Shertallai and Thrippunithura, the Cochin dynasty's mother-house, appointing his own officials. In April Poku Mussa demands the princes of Tekkumkur and Desinganadu, with 3,000 troops waiting in Vadakkumkur and Tekkumkur.

The Brahmin court finds for the Tamban on the title and its revenues; he wants the throne too, and Martanda Varma sends reinforcements. At year's end the Tamban allies by adoption with Koratti Kaimal.

In September exiled Tekkumkur princes fail to retake the fort of Kottayam. In October the Brahmin prince of Purakkad loses his lands and lives as a renouncer under house arrest at Kudumalur; Travancore officials take the pepper.
Martanda Varma finally performs the hiranyagarbha, the 'great gift' of rebirth from a golden cow whose gold goes to the Nambuthiri, and from then wears the sacred thread.

Signed where Ramayyan's great commercial department sits, almost twelve years after Colachel's fall. Travancore will sell the Dutch all its cotton and 5,000 candies of pepper a year: 3,000 from Travancore and Attingal at 65 rupees, 2,000 from lands still to be conquered at 55, so the Dutch in effect accept future conquests. The Dutch supply 12,000 rupees of arms a year and iron cannon, help against other Europeans, and promise strict neutrality if Kerala princes fight Travancore. A ceasefire binds Cochin to pay 25,000 rupees and sell Travancore all pepper but 500 candies.
q: he does not care for his neighbours and plays with them as a cat with a mouse with the object to gain the profits from this game
src: Cochin king to the Governor-General, 14 Oct 1753; VOC 2815

x: Martanda Varma pays off the debts Desinganadu and the Tekkumkur princes owe the Dutch and takes their pawned jewels, the marks of princely authority.

t: The northern princes rise; Mavelikara falls
x: Vadakkumkur's civil war resumes; its minister Eddaddy Comy, arrested at Trivandrum, escapes and the princes unite with Tekkumkur at Vaikom. They beat the Travancoreans at Adirampose, take Ettumanur and Kunrattu, reach Changanacherri to a welcome from merchants tired of the pepper monopoly, then march south and take Mavelikara with its warehouses of pepper and money. Ten years of expansion seem undone. Cochin stops paying and courts the Madurai governor Moodemiah; the Zamorin refuses Travancore's tribute demand and turns to the French at Mahé.

At the Irinjalakkuda temple the great Cochin nobles settle their feuds and vote 20,000 men under the second prince of Cochin, who expels the Travancoreans from Shertallai and sets up at Alleppey. Christians are conscripted against the 1663 treaty. The old Desinganadu, in exile at Kottayam in Cannanur, will not join; he dies in 1754.

When the Nawab of Trichinopoly replaces Moodemiah, Moodemiah allies with Travancore and returns the forts of Valliyur and Kalakad. Freed in the south, Martanda Varma retakes Mavelikara and pushes the allies back to Changanacherri, his new headquarters. 'Three factors were crucial': his health, the monsoon and events in Madurai.

The captive Purakkad prince calls the Cochin nobles to Ambalapuzha and the allies fortify Tottapolli just south of it. Unable to storm the lines, Martanda Varma bribes general Mattur Panikkar and the family priest Tekkedattu Bhattan to say Travancore is withdrawing, then they let his troops in. Six Cochin nobles are captured; two are poisoned at Trivandrum, four freed as tributaries. Ramayyan takes over Purakkad's government.

The Zamorin invades Cochin from the north, pulling Cochin troops out of Vadakkumkur and Tekkumkur. Travancore invades, but 10,000 men fight a forest guerrilla war that a European-style army handles badly. In the monsoon the king has a wall of hard earth built from Vaikom to the Ghats, more than 33 km long, 3 to 4 m thick, with bastions every 2 km for four to eight guns; nearly 8,000 men from Kayamkulam and Mavelikara build it under artillery cover. Armed boats guard the Cochin river.

Travancore crosses into Cochin's Mutton province via Purakkad and occupies Karappuram; east of the river it takes Kuttamperur, Edawaga and Putotta. Then it stops: in March the Nawab Muhammad Ali reaches Tinnevelly with English auxiliaries under colonel Heron. English carpenters build Travancore an armed ship in exchange for pepper.

After the allies force a reconciliation of the Tamban and the Cochin king at Thrippunithura, Travancore attacks. Armed vessels clear the Cochin river; Tripose and Wallarimangalam fall; Thrippunithura is taken and the Kandanad bazaar, churches and palaces are burnt. The Cochin royal family flees north with its treasure. In the east Managunattu, the hub of pepper smuggled by ox over the passes that paid Tekkumkur's 6,000 men, is taken and the prince retreats into the Ghats.

t: De Lannoy beats the Nawab's army
x: When the Nawab's troops cross the border, 2,000 or 3,000 Travancore elite troops under Eustache de Lannoy drive them back, taking four heavy cannon, flints, horses and oxen and burning their camp. The Nawab withdraws to Tinnevelly. A Tekkumkur counter-attack fails.

Ramayyan, one of the architects of expansion, dies. Next month Todupuzha, Vadakkumkur's last stronghold, falls and its elite troops leave service. Todupuzha, Ettumanur, Kottayam and Changanacherri are fortified in western style by Europeans such as De Lannoy. Alangadu, Parur and Cranganur fear they are next; the Dutch ask Travancore to stay 10 km from Cochin.
note: The same page also says Todupuzha was lost in January 1756.

x: Cochin would give Travancore all pepper but 500 candies, accept the occupation of Tekkumkur and Vadakkumkur, and give the exiles no refuge; Travancore would win back land lost to the Zamorin. The Purakkad prince may live at the Trichur temple, forbidden to write or receive letters. The Zamorin's intrigues sink it; in October he offers the Dutch 2,000 candies to join him.

The kings of Travancore and Cochin meet at the Thrippunithura temple. By custom Martanda Varma may not sit before the Cochin king, head of the chovvaram faction; he stands against a pillar while the Cochin king leans on a noble. After a long silence Martanda Varma heaps complaints on him; the Cochin king apologises and falls silent. Cochin's lands are run by Travancore governors and its produce bought cheap.

Travancore and Zamorin envoys meet secretly at the Trichur temple; the Dutch fear a plan to divide Cochin and attack their forts. Poku Mussa, protecting a tax collector who seizes Christian fishermen's nets, turns away the Dutch presents. In October he offers the Dutch an alliance against the Zamorin.
The Zamorin and the Dutch end the hostilities that began late in 1756, heading off a Travancore-led coalition.
Martanda Varma dies. By then he has ended the old order in Travancore and the old Kerala system of states as far north as the Zamorin's border.
The torakar of the Suchindram temple make an acarakkanakku, an account of the temple's ceremonies and their costs, an early step in royal scrutiny of temple wealth.

Pieter Lodder, chief of Paravur, is impressed by the discipline of 50,000 Travancore soldiers passing with oxen, horses and elephants. The same month the Dutch sneer that the army is 'much more badly trained than that of Persia shortly after the revolution'.
src: Lodder to Hendrix, 23 Apr 1732; VOC 2231

t: Cotton duties offered to the Dutch
x: Martanda Varma tries to farm the duties on cotton to the Dutch, assessing them at 130,000 kaliyan panam. He also posts a tax-collector at the gate of Anjengo so all English goods are taxed.
src: Arumukkan Pillai to Hendrix, 16 Apr 1732; VOC 2231

x: A letter from Tengapattanam proves the king has ordered a large quantity of gabions, siege baskets of European type. A mestizo gunner who deserted from Anjengo serves him.

t: No Dutchmen left in his service
x: Wars against Quilon and Kayamkulam have emptied the treasury; unpaid Europeans have died or left, so the king can truly say he has no Dutchmen serving him.

Small armed vessels cruise the backwaters exacting tolls, even from ships with VOC passes; boarders tear up Dutch passes and destroy Dutch flags. Cochin reports the king has cash problems yet keeps a large standing army.
src: Cochin Council to Batavia, 24 Apr 1735; VOC 2339

t: A land tax, the first in Travancore
x: Rather than raise customs further, prime minister Thanu Pillai introduces an irregular assessment of land, levied in kind and money. Only Brahmins and temples are exempt.
Thanu Pillai dies. His successor Ramayyan is a Tamil Brahmin born in Tirunelveli district who came to Trivandrum aged six as a boy servant at the Sri Padmanabha temple.
Lines are built against the annual Madurai tribute raids. Customs at Colachel rise; the English complain of its port farmer.

t: Van Imhoff inspects the southern lines
x: He finds a badly made ditch and walls of hard earth on stone foundations, 12 to 15 feet high, too long to defend, with no artillery anywhere.
q: The lines were so long that it was impossible to defend them effectively. Nowhere artillery was seen.
src: Diary Van Imhoff, 5 Mar 1739; VOC 2472

t: Martanda Varma asks the French for help
x: In the middle of the Dutch war he writes to Dirois at Mahé for military aid; a year later he works the English the same way. Court splits into a French faction under the Pandalam prince and an English one under Krishna Anavy.

t: Mercenaries flee to Anjengo and are sent back
x: When the Dutch land at Colachel, Dutch mercenaries in Travancore service flee to Anjengo. The king threatens to cut off its food; the English return them.
To legitimise the land tax and tighter control of temple land, the king pays homage at the Adi Kesava temple at Tiruvattar and consecrates his sword to it.

At seven or eight in the morning the survivors march out under full colours, armed. 500 steps outside they are stopped at the bankshall, told to give up their arms, refuse, and are made prisoner. Stripped almost naked and beaten, they are driven 11 km over the beach to Cariapattanam, where 5,000 soldiers have orders to kill them.
src: Secret relaas of sergeant Jan Christoffel Hartman, 16 Dec 1741; VOC 2523

x: Ill in bed at Iranyal, Duijvenschot threatens the king that he and the other Europeans will take revenge if the prisoners are killed. The king's kariyakar, too exhausted to go himself, sends a dubash servant whom the soldiers will not believe; he holds off the killing until his master arrives with the king's ola. In the evening each prisoner gets a piece of jaggery.

t: Prisoners before the king at Paterre
x: Given trousers, a camisole and a handkerchief, the prisoners meet the king at his temporary residence at Paterre. Duijvenschot says they all want to serve him; the king orders them treated kindly and sent to Iranyal fort. 40 wounded follow by vallam under bookkeeper Karel Hendrix; Meran Pillai Mether carries off the guns. De Lannoy could not find Paterre on any map.
note: Paterre is unidentified; the author writes 'I could not found Paterre on the map'.

x: Duijvenschot greets them: 'It is a pity that you have lost the battle, but I am happy that you are still alive.' Two days later the second prince asks them to serve; they refuse, citing the capitulation. Duijvenschot then withdraws their privileges until hunger and fear drive all into Travancore service. Hartman is made ensign.
q: I did nothing out of enmity against the Hon. Company but I still entertain bitter feelings towards some of the Dutch officers who treated us, common soldiers, as scoundrels and riff-raff

x: Rewarded for Colachel and for enlisting Europeans, he commands 30,000 men, 4,000 or 5,000 with European firearms, spread across the country but able to unite at Attingal within two days. The king sends De Lannoy to Mahé to ask the French for help, which displeases the pro-English Duijvenschot.

t: Duijvenschot ill at Anjengo; the surgeon escapes
x: Mentally deranged by a tropical disease, Duijvenschot is received at Anjengo 'with all honours' by Charles Whitehill and treated, on pain of death, by the captured Dutch surgeon Rosenvelt, who escapes to Seeburg on 27 November. A Dutch party sent to seize Duijvenschot finds him gone. Two recaptured runaways are tied to poles on the beach and shot.
Cochin reports the king has raised the levy on landed property from 30 to 100 kaliyan panam a year to pay his Europeans; 'this king has exhausted his treasury'.
src: Cochin Council to Batavia, 20 Mar 1742; VOC 2577

t: De Lannoy trains the palace guard
x: In three months De Lannoy drills the king's palace guard, dressed and armed like Europeans, so well that the Madurai troops can be sent home, saving 60,000 rupees a month. He becomes its commander and Venattu Kappittan, Captain of Venad. General conscription follows and the old kalari fencing schools are revived.
src: Cochin Council to Batavia, 6 Nov 1742; VOC 2561

x: The Mavelikara treaty's pepper quota can only be met if the state controls all pepper: it becomes a monopoly, run by Ramayyan from Mavelikara with storehouses and depots across the country and a fixed budget, the pathivu-kanakku, used into the twentieth century.

After the peace the king returns unwilling Dutchmen but keeps volunteers, saying the VOC would hang them. Siersma says a hundred Mendeses could not find them, warns that 'la Nooy' is no better than Duijvenschot, and receives instead a large trained brown bear. Nearly 40 Europeans remain in Travancore service.
src: Cochin Diary, entry of 24 Mar 1744; VOC 2624

x: The king builds a new summer residence at Kalkulam, later Padmanabhapuram. De Lannoy rebuilds Udayagiri fort in brick: about 36 ha around a 79 m hill, walls 4.5 m thick and over 5 m high faced with granite, 10 bastions. It becomes the seat of the Valiya Kappittan, an arms works and the state prison.

Margaret's father, a Syrian Christian interpreter for the king and the English at Anjengo, refuses a French deserter who trains half-naked natives for a heathen prince. The king threatens to destroy Anjengo unless the English make him consent. The couple settle at Udayagiri.
note: The marriage date is 'probably in 1744'; the account rests on Anquetil du Perron.

x: After a long and painful illness. Siersma calls it God's just punishment and expects the Europeans to melt away under 'a certain Benedictus de Lanoy'. Instead the army grows stronger.
src: Cochin Council to Batavia, 2 May 1744; VOC 2624

t: Krishna Anavy's arms deal at Anjengo
x: He asks the English for one musket per candy of pepper sold, plus 15,000 flints, 30 candies of lead, saltpetre, brimstone, 200 mortar shells and 500 cannon balls a year. The English fail to deliver and the king turns to the French.

t: Suchindram lands leased to the state
x: The Suchindram temple is forced to lease part of its estates to the state on long-term submortgage, widening the land producing for state monopolies.
Joannes Eustachius Benedictus de Lannoy, the 'Small Captain', is born, probably at Udayagiri.
From the end of 1745 Martanda Varma is ill and leans more and more on Ramayyan.

Piece-goods become a state monopoly. Duijvenschot and De Lannoy rebuild the Aramboli Lines in brick with parapets and ramparts; after 1746 they run from the coastal fort of Vattakotta west of Kanniyakumari, via Chevery Kotta, to Aramboli fort with its arsenals, held by the Eastern Brigade.
Two French ships come to Colachel; the English hear of a joint attack on Desinganadu in exchange for a factory. From March ministers of the French faction write secretly to the French.

t: Van der Linden visits the Jesuit archbishop
x: Investigating Jesuit help to deserters, he visits archbishop Anthony Pimentel at Ambalakadu, who says his French, Portuguese and British guests are shipwrecked sailors looking for work. No proof is found.

t: English families to shelter at Iranyal
x: After Madras falls to the French (10 September) and a French and Angria fleet is rumoured against Anjengo, the king agrees to protect English women and children in Iranyal fort, for a loan of 10,000 kaliyan panam partly spent on old English cannon.

t: A friar's letter to De Lannoy intercepted
x: A Catholic father at Alakarkovil recommends two French Catholic deserters to 'the captain of Travancore', De Lannoy, as his compatriots. Cochin sends a translation to Batavia on 12 February.
src: Translaet van een Portugees Briefje, 3 Jan 1748; VOC 2713

t: Eleven men go over the Cochin walls
x: Eleven soldiers desert by night with their flintlocks. An alarm gun is heard at Ernakulam, whose kaimal reports them; 37 men are sent with a 120 rixdollar reward and catch two in the hill forest, one shot in the buttocks.
Martanda Varma gives his weight in gold to the Brahmins, a gift required of a kulasekhara perumal. In 1748 and June 1749 De Lannoy receives 2,900 kaliyan panam in pay and rewards.

t: The kingdom given to Sri Padmanabha
x: With pomp the king dedicates all Travancore to the god. The state becomes sri pandaravaka, the god's property; he becomes Sri Padmanabha Dasa, the god's servant. The line between royal and temple land disappears and the Edappalli priest-prince loses his independence. The silver chakram, stamped with Vishnu's wheel, follows; any act against the king is now blasphemy.
Travancore buys large quantities of red cloth at Anjengo for the kunju kudis' uniforms. In July twelve Tekkumkur pepper smugglers have their noses and ears cut off.

t: The English seize the Kolathiri king
x: The English carry the aged Kolathiri king to Tellicherri by force, annoying his kinsman Martanda Varma; the Dutch use it to win him back, leading to the 1753 treaty.
At the Mavelikara conference the king asks the Dutch to recognise him as kulasekhara perumal, 'Emperor of Malabar', having performed every rite. They refuse.
src: Report of the Mavelikara conference, 18 Aug 1753; VOC 2815

x: After Ramayyan's death courtiers and governors fight over his post, among them the Syrian Christian rivals Poku Mussa and Mathu Tharakan; it stays vacant until the king's death.
Merchants bringing tobacco from Jaffna must sell to the state and buy pepper from it at 120 rupees a candy.

t: Poku Mussa trampled by an elephant
x: The new king Rama Varma, the Dharma Raja, strips Poku Mussa of office and has him trampled to death at Purakkad, confiscating 200,000 rupees of property. Mathu Tharakan rises.
De Lannoy arrests Cochin pearl-fishers near Kanniyakumari; the king claims the banks of Manakkudi and Kovalam. The Dutch blame De Lannoy and two Catholic priests at court.

After the Cochin alliance, the Nedumkotta is begun: over 56 km from Kuriappalli on the coast into the Ghats, with a ditch 6 m deep, 20 bastions and camps every 3 km, held by the new Northern Brigade at Alleppey. In 1790 Tipu Sultan needs six months to take it.

t: The Cheriya Kappittan killed at Kalakad
x: De Lannoy's son dies in battle, not yet 20. His father builds a Catholic chapel in Udayagiri fort in his memory.

t: Mahé still asks De Lannoy's favour
x: The French chief Picot de La Motte asks him to use his influence for better French trade terms, a sign he is still heard at court despite illness.

After 36 years serving two kings, he is buried with military honours in his chapel under a tombstone carved with his arms, a cannon, drums, muskets and two angels in mixed European and Indian style, titled 'Dux generalissimus'. Pierre Fleury succeeds him (d. 16 Mar 1780), then Joseph Donnadi.
Known for charity to the poor and still paid her husband's salary by Rama Varma, she is buried beside him and their son.

Rama Varma allies with the English, who post a resident and troops behind the Lines; all Frenchmen leave the army. Three Nayar Brigades remain: Northern under Martanda Pillai, Eastern ('French') and Southern under Claude Fleury.

The dewan Velu Tambi rises against the English; he is killed and 'with him Travancore as an independent state disappeared'. Colonel Welsh finds at Udayagiri a brass gun 16 feet long that 1,200 men and 16 elephants could not move.
